# Discussion 344
As a result of our work, we propose the use of SDEvelo for quantifying RNA velocity for multiple 345 genes simultaneously in a manner governed by cell-specific latent times. Unlike methods that 346 model the RNA velocity of each gene with gene-specific latent time using univariate ODE, 347 SDEvelo explicitly models the RNA velocity of multiple genes governed by the cell-specific 348 latent time while considering the inherent stochastic nature of the dynamics that account for 349 the randomness of biological processes during transcription using SDE. Moreover, SDEvelo 350 uses nonlinear but differentiable sigmoid functions for the transcription rate to gradually and 351 smoothly model expression changes, instead of using indicator functions that show instant 352 changes. All these considerations mean SDEvelo provides reliable and robust velocity and 353 latent time estimations. 354

Conventionally, solving SDE requires temporal information for each data point, which is 355 largely missing from sequencing data. Taking advantage of the successes of both deep generative 356 models and adversarial learning, SDEvelo infers all parameters via a strategy that minimizes 357 the divergence between the real input data and the data generated by the SDE model. In the 358 data-generation steps, the Euler-Maruyama method is used to discretize the continuous SDE 359 process and generate trajectories based on the current model. 360

With a PBMC dataset and simulations, we demonstrated that SDEvelo can mitigate the 361 long-standing problem of the erroneous directions inferred by existing methods for mature-state 362 cells. In cells sampled from populations in mature states, we expect to observe a noisy velocity 363 field without a clear direction. Among the PBMC and simulated datasets, only SDEvelo 364 estimated a noisy, directionless velocity field, while the others erroneously inferred particular 365 directions within the t -SNE representation. Additionally, SDEvelo is applicable to datasets 366 generated using various sequencing-based technologies, including sequencing-based spatial 367 transcriptomics data of low depth. From a dataset of four HCC sections generated using 10x 368 Visium, SDEvelo correctly estimated the velocity directions and latent times in both tumor 369 and tumor-adjacent tissues, facilitating the detection of cancer driver genes in HCC, as well 370 as constructing a PPI network. Further analysis of pairwise correlations between these genes 371 suggested their strong enrichment in liver-related cancers. 372

SDEvelo provides a systematic solution for the rapidly developing area of RNA velocity. 373 First, although SDEvelo can be applied to spatial transcriptomics data, it does not model spatial 374 information explicitly. The desired velocity method should account for both spatial locations 375 and various spatial resolutions. Secondly, it would be interesting to apply the computational 376 framework of SDEvelo to the integration of other modality data within single-cell genomics 377 with a time-dependent transcription rate. 378
# Methods 379

# Modeling Stochastic Kinetics with SDEvelo 380
As in conventional RNA velocity analyses, the transcriptional kinetics for each gene were 381 modeled by a deterministic and gene-gene-independent ODE system, 382

du ( t ) dt = α ( t ) -βu ( t ) , ds ( t ) dt = βu ( t ) -γs ( t ) . (2)

The ODE system delineates the dynamics of unspliced transcripts, u ( t ), and spliced transcripts, 383 s ( t ), over time. The transcription rate, denoted by α ( t ), is commonly approximated by a step384 wise indicator function [12, 13]. β and γ represent the scalar parameters for the rates of splicing 385 and degradation, respectively. However, this ODE-based model has three limitations: (1) It 386 delineates a deterministic process that cannot capture the intrinsic randomness of transcriptional 387 dynamics; (2) The step-wise transcription function is non-differentiable and suggests an 388 intermediate transition between induction and repression phases; and (3) The univariate system 389 of ODE equations models the transcriptional dynamics for each gene independently, without 390 consideration of the interactive regulatory pathways acting across multiple genes. 391

Here, we present a model overview of SDEvelo, and further details are available in the 392 Supplementary Notes. Consider the multivariate state variables U ( t ) and S ( t ) in all p genes, 393 which represent the dynamics for unspliced and spliced transcripts, respectively, over a cell394 specific latent time t . With p genes, we assume the corresponding p -dimensional vectors 395 for transcription rates, splicing rates, and degradation rates α ( t ) = ( α ( t ) 1 , . . . , α ( t ) p ) /latticetop , β = 396 ( β 1 , . . . , β p ) /latticetop , and γ = ( γ 1 , . . . , γ p ) /latticetop . Without loss of generality, we assume t ∈ [0 , 1] describes 397 a finite period, and SDEvelo models the unspliced and spliced transcripts, U ( t ) and S ( t ), 398

- respectively, as in Eqn. (1), with a Wiener process that accounts for both the intrinsic and 399 extrinsic noises of unspliced and spliced transcripts. 400
- For transcription function α ( t ), we consider differentiable sigmoid functions to avoid 401 describing intermediate transitional states between two phases, 402

α ( t ) i = c i 1 + exp { b ( t -a i ) } , i = 1 , . . . , p, (3)

where a = ( a 1 , . . . , a p ) /latticetop is a vector of the switch time points, c = ( c 1 , . . . , c p ) /latticetop is a vector of 403 the transcription rates of all p genes, and b is the hyperparameter used to tune the shape of 404 the sigmoid function. The curves for the different values of b in the sigmoid functions, along 405 with the original indicator function, are shown in Fig. 1b. 406

# Adversarial learning parameters 407
In practice, resolving multivariate ODE/SDE remains challenging. Most univariate ODE-based 408 methods utilize the EM algorithm to infer model parameters, for which the explicit solutions of 409 ODE are essentially required during iterations [13, 15, 20]. However, for nonlinearly coupled mul410 tivariate SDE, it is difficult to obtain explicit solutions. SDEvelo estimates the model parameters 411 by adversarially comparing real and generated data from the SDE, and the Euler-Maruyama 412 method [53, 54] is used to discretize the continuous SDE process and generate trajectories from 413 the current iteration. The parameters are updated by stochastic gradient descent, minimizing 414 divergence loss with the incorporation of the transcription/splicing/degradation rate, as well as 415 the noise levels that characterize both the extrinsic and intrinsic stochasticity. 416

The flowchart for estimating the parameters in SDEvelo is displayed in Supplementary 417 Fig. S1. SDEvelo adversarially estimates the parameters for the combination of stochastic 418 gradient descent and generative modeling by minimizing the divergence between the distributions 419 obtained from real data and those from SDE-generated data using the maximum mean 420 discrepancy (MMD) [55, 56], for which the core functions of SDEvelo are in line with the 421 generative adversarial networks of deep learning [57]. 422

To generate trajectories from SDE, we used the Euler-Maruyama method [53, 54] to obtain 423 the discretized observations from the continuous diffusion process as 424

where Z 1 , Z 2 ∼ N (0 , 1). Denote the set of unknown parameters as Θ = { a , c , β , γ , σ 1 , σ 2 } , 425 which dominates the generated trajectories of the transaction process. We estimated Θ by 426 minimizing the empirical MMD objective with the kernel trick, 427

The divergence measures the discrepancy between two datasets: the first consists of N g cell 428 samples, G (Θ) = { g i (Θ) } N g i =1 , generated from SDE trajectories; the second comprises N r real 429 cell samples, R = { r j } N r j =1 , where each g i ∈ R 2 p is a concatenated vector of unspliced and spliced 430

data for p genes in cell i , and each r j ∈ R 2 p represents the real data for the corresponding 431 cell. In the kernel trick, we chose the Gaussian kernel k ( x, x ′ ) = ∑ K q =1 exp ( -1 2 w q | x -x ′ | 2 ) , 432 combining different bandwidth parameters w q . Since the MMD loss (5) is differentiable, we 433 applied stochastic gradient descent to minimize the loss of function (5) and estimate parameters 434 Θ [58, 59]. Thus, the computational framework is scalable and applicable to both CPU and 435 GPU platforms. Further details on the implementation are provided in the Supplementary 436 Notes. 437

# Estimation of latent time 438
To infer latent time in SDEvelo, we used the estimated SDE with these generated points. In 439 detail, we first generated trajectories from the SDE with the inferred parameters. Then, using 440 the idea of optimal transport, we matched the generated trajectories with the real observed 441 data. 442

We used G (Θ) to denote the trajectories generated from SDEvelo using the inferred 443 parameters Θ, with R for the observed data. Assuming that each point g i (Θ) ∈ G (Θ) is 444 governed by a time t i in SDEvelo, we aimed to identify a bijection φ : G (Θ) → R that 445 minimizes the total cost of transportation. Formally, this can be defined as follows: 446

φ ∗ = arg min φ : G (Θ) → R N g ∑ i =1 | g i (Θ) -φ ( g i (Θ)) | 2 , (6)

where |·| 2 denotes a squared Euclidean distance. After obtaining the optimal bijection φ ∗ , each 447 observed point r i = φ ( g i (Θ)) was assigned a latent time t i from its corresponding generated 448 point g i (Θ). By estimating the cell-specific latent time across multiple genes, SDEvelo can 449 reveal the temporal progression of cell differentiation processes. 450

# Abstract
Recently, RNA velocity has driven a paradigmatic change in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) studies, allowing the reconstruction and prediction of directed trajectories in cell differentiation and state transitions. However, most existing methods use dynamic modeling via ordinary differential equations (ODE) for individual genes in sequence and can lead to erroneous results, as they are inadequately able to fully capture the intrinsically stochastic nature of transcriptional dynamics governed by a cell-specific latent time across multiple genes. Here, we present SDEvelo, a novel deep generative approach to inferring RNA velocity by modeling the dynamics of unspliced and spliced RNAs via multivariate stochastic differential equations (SDE). Uniquely, SDEvelo explicitly models inherent uncertainty in transcriptional dynamics while estimating a cell-specific latent time across

genes. Using both simulated and four scRNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics datasets, we 30 show that SDEvelo can model the random dynamic patterns of mature-state cells while 31 accurately detecting carcinogenesis. Additionally, the estimated gene-shared latent time 32 can facilitate many downstream analyses for biological discovery. We demonstrate that 33 SDEvelo is computationally scalable and applicable to both scRNA-seq and sequencing34 based spatial transcriptomics data. 35

# Introduction 36
- The advent of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has revolutionized our understanding of 37
- molecular and cellular processes. It offers unprecedented opportunities to explore gene expression 38

- the developmental paths of individual cells over time [3-7]. A major challenge in trajectory 42
- inference is the destructive nature of scRNA-seq, which captures only a static snapshot of 43
- the transcriptome of cellular states at the moment of measurement. Therefore, conventional 44
- trajectory inference methods require enough cells to be profiled from all intermediate states 45
- to enable the reconstruction of continuous trajectories [8], and prior knowledge is needed to 46

- the cell fates are unknown. 49

- transcription of pre-mRNAs, their conversion into spliced mRNAs, and eventual degradation, 53
- RNA velocity can be inferred. A positive velocity indicates a gene being up-regulated in 54
- spliced transcripts whilst a negative velocity indicates down-regulation. Assuming that the 55
- transcriptional phases of the induction and repression of gene expression last sufficiently long 56

- An ideal RNA velocity method should be capable of tackling the following three tasks: (1) 62

# Discussion 344
As a result of our work, we propose the use of SDEvelo for quantifying RNA velocity for multiple 345 genes simultaneously in a manner governed by cell-specific latent times. Unlike methods that 346 model the RNA velocity of each gene with gene-specific latent time using univariate ODE, 347 SDEvelo explicitly models the RNA velocity of multiple genes governed by the cell-specific 348 latent time while considering the inherent stochastic nature of the dynamics that account for 349 the randomness of biological processes during transcription using SDE. Moreover, SDEvelo 350 uses nonlinear but differentiable sigmoid functions for the transcription rate to gradually and 351 smoothly model expression changes, instead of using indicator functions that show instant 352 changes. All these considerations mean SDEvelo provides reliable and robust velocity and 353 latent time estimations. 354

Conventionally, solving SDE requires temporal information for each data point, which is 355 largely missing from sequencing data. Taking advantage of the successes of both deep generative 356 models and adversarial learning, SDEvelo infers all parameters via a strategy that minimizes 357 the divergence between the real input data and the data generated by the SDE model. In the 358 data-generation steps, the Euler-Maruyama method is used to discretize the continuous SDE 359 process and generate trajectories based on the current model. 360

With a PBMC dataset and simulations, we demonstrated that SDEvelo can mitigate the 361 long-standing problem of the erroneous directions inferred by existing methods for mature-state 362 cells. In cells sampled from populations in mature states, we expect to observe a noisy velocity 363 field without a clear direction. Among the PBMC and simulated datasets, only SDEvelo 364 estimated a noisy, directionless velocity field, while the others erroneously inferred particular 365 directions within the t -SNE representation. Additionally, SDEvelo is applicable to datasets 366 generated using various sequencing-based technologies, including sequencing-based spatial 367 transcriptomics data of low depth. From a dataset of four HCC sections generated using 10x 368 Visium, SDEvelo correctly estimated the velocity directions and latent times in both tumor 369 and tumor-adjacent tissues, facilitating the detection of cancer driver genes in HCC, as well 370 as constructing a PPI network. Further analysis of pairwise correlations between these genes 371 suggested their strong enrichment in liver-related cancers. 372

SDEvelo provides a systematic solution for the rapidly developing area of RNA velocity. 373 First, although SDEvelo can be applied to spatial transcriptomics data, it does not model spatial 374 information explicitly. The desired velocity method should account for both spatial locations 375 and various spatial resolutions. Secondly, it would be interesting to apply the computational 376 framework of SDEvelo to the integration of other modality data within single-cell genomics 377 with a time-dependent transcription rate. 378

# Adversarial learning parameters 407
In practice, resolving multivariate ODE/SDE remains challenging. Most univariate ODE-based 408 methods utilize the EM algorithm to infer model parameters, for which the explicit solutions of 409 ODE are essentially required during iterations [13, 15, 20]. However, for nonlinearly coupled mul410 tivariate SDE, it is difficult to obtain explicit solutions. SDEvelo estimates the model parameters 411 by adversarially comparing real and generated data from the SDE, and the Euler-Maruyama 412 method [53, 54] is used to discretize the continuous SDE process and generate trajectories from 413 the current iteration. The parameters are updated by stochastic gradient descent, minimizing 414 divergence loss with the incorporation of the transcription/splicing/degradation rate, as well as 415 the noise levels that characterize both the extrinsic and intrinsic stochasticity. 416

The flowchart for estimating the parameters in SDEvelo is displayed in Supplementary 417 Fig. S1. SDEvelo adversarially estimates the parameters for the combination of stochastic 418 gradient descent and generative modeling by minimizing the divergence between the distributions 419 obtained from real data and those from SDE-generated data using the maximum mean 420 discrepancy (MMD) [55, 56], for which the core functions of SDEvelo are in line with the 421 generative adversarial networks of deep learning [57]. 422
